glossary.title: Generative AI
glossary.summary: AI systems that produce new content (text, images, audio, code) from learned distributions.
glossary.body: Generative AI refers to machine-learning systems trained to synthesize novel outputs that reflect patterns in their training data. Prominent examples include large language models, diffusion image models, and code-generation assistants. In the enterprise, generative AI underpins content automation, copilots, and agent workflows.

glossary.title: Large Language Model (LLM)
glossary.summary: A neural model with billions of parameters trained on large text corpora to predict and generate language.
glossary.body: A Large Language Model is a transformer-based neural network trained on broad text corpora at scale, used for generation, summarization, retrieval, classification, and agentic tool use. Enterprise adoption depends on governance, evaluation, and retrieval-augmentation controls.

glossary.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
glossary.summary: A pattern that grounds model generation in documents retrieved at query time.
glossary.body: Retrieval-Augmented Generation combines a retriever (often vector search over an index) with a generator (an LLM) so the model's answer is grounded in fetched source passages, improving factual accuracy and source attribution.

glossary.title: Quantum Computing
glossary.summary: Computation that uses quantum-mechanical phenomena (superposition, entanglement) to process information.
glossary.body: Quantum computing uses qubits, which can exist in superpositions of states, enabling algorithms (e.g., Shor, Grover) that can outperform classical counterparts on specific problems. It remains largely experimental, with hardware from superconducting, trapped-ion, and photonic platforms.

glossary.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC)
glossary.summary: Cryptographic algorithms believed secure against large-scale quantum attacks.
glossary.body: Post-Quantum Cryptography comprises cryptographic schemes (lattice-, code-, hash-, and isogeny-based) designed to resist attacks by large quantum computers. NIST has standardized selected PQC algorithms; migration requires cryptographic agility.
